# Education in Poland
Education in Poland begins with compulsory primary school (szkoła podstawowa) attendance at age six or seven, typically lasting eight years (grades 1–8). Before 2017, primary education was six years followed by three years of mandatory junior high school (gimnazjum), which was abolished starting from the 2017 reform. This reform extended primary school to eight years and adjusted upper secondary education accordingly. The former gimnazjum covered lower secondary education with a curriculum including Polish language, history, sciences, foreign languages, and more, culminating in evaluations and examinations.
Upper secondary education comprises general secondary schools (liceum), technical schools (technikum), and basic vocational schools (zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa). General secondary schools last four years and lead to the Matura examination, which qualifies students for higher education. Technical schools last five years, also culminating in the Matura, and focus on trades such as accounting and mechanics. Basic vocational schools provide three years of vocational education with certification but no Matura unless followed by further schooling. Vocational and specialized schools serve physically or mentally handicapped students.
Poland's tertiary education follows the Bologna process with mostly three-year bachelor's degrees followed by two-year master's degrees, though some programs (e.g., medicine, pharmacy) are long-cycle lasting up to six years. Doctoral studies typically last about three years. University grading uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (highest), sometimes with half-point increments. Students usually learn one or two foreign languages, predominantly English, German, and French. Recent reforms have altered curricula focus and structure, with some concerns about nationalistic and Eurocentric content adjustments.
